newsitem.title: USA: U.S. JUDGES ORDERS THREE EXTRADITED TO BRITAIN.
newsitem.headline: U.S. JUDGES ORDERS THREE EXTRADITED TO BRITAIN.

text.p: A U.S. judge on Monday ordered three escapees from a prison in Northern Ireland extradited to Britain, finding they would not be punished for their political views if returned to British custody.
Kevin Artt, Pol Brennan and Terence Kirby, who all escaped from Northern Ireland's Maze prison in 1983, were arrested in California between 1992 and 1994.

Artt and Kirby were convicted in Northern Ireland of murder, and Brennan was convicted there on explosives charges. They are accused by Britain of links to the Irish Republican Army, which has waged a guerrilla campaign to end British rule in Northern Ireland.

The men opposed a British extradition request, invoking a clause of the U.S.-British extradition treaty that bars extradition when people would be punished because of race, religion or political opinions if extradited.
But U.S. District Judge Charles Legge rejected their arguments in a written ruling released several months after the extradition hearings.
"Respondents were convicted because they committed serious crimes, not because they are Catholics or Nationalists or Republicans," Legge wrote.
"A killing is still a crime, regardless of the banner under which the criminal stands when he kills," he said.

"And if returned to Northern Ireland, respondents' further punishment will not be because of their beliefs, but because of the crimes which they committed," he said, certifying that Artt, Brennan and Kirby could be extradited.
He ordered the three men, who had been free on bail, to surrender to U.S. marshals immediately.
"The historical context in which these cases arose in Northern Ireland is a tragedy -- of history, of politics and of religion. ... This court has no power to change that history," Legge wrote.

Artt, arriving at the federal courthouse in San Francisco to surrender, said he was "totally and utterly shocked" by the ruling. Asked what he believed would happen to him if he went back to prison in Northern Ireland, he said, "I'll end up dead one way or the other unless this (Northern Ireland) peace process is able to somehow turn things around."
The IRA called a ceasefire three weeks ago to get its political wing, Sinn Fein, into peace talks to end a conflict that has killed 3,200 people.
Artt's attorneys said they were seeking his release on bail pending the outcome of an appeal to a federal appeals court. The other two men were also expected to appeal.
"We're delighted that the U.S. courts have rendered a decision to extradite the three," Kevin Cook, a spokesman for the British consulate in San Francisco, said.
Artt, Brennan and Kirby were among 38 prisoners who escaped from the Maze prison in the largest jailbreak in British history. They had been living in California under false names until their arrest.

Artt was convicted in 1983 of the 1978 murder of Albert Miles, the deputy governor of the Maze Prison. Artt maintained that he was innocent and that his conviction was based entirely on his involuntary confession.
At the extradition hearing, his attorney, James Brosnahan, said Artt was convicted in a "trumped-up" case. He said Artt was an "IRA wannabe" but had never joined the organisation.
Kirby contested one of his convictions, while Brennan did not deny that he was guilty of the crime of which he was convicted, according to the U.S. court record.
Another Maze escapee, Jimmy Smyth, was extradited last August after losing a four-year legal battle to stay in the United States.
